Honzō Zufu (Illustrated Materia Medica)

Preface to the Honzō Zufu

All the countless transformations and growth of plants and animals between Heaven and Earth cannot be reckoned in their thousands and hundreds. Their forms are strange and varied, great and small intermingled, as vast and boundless as a misty sea. There are things that brush and ink records cannot fully capture in their intricate detail — and so they are entrusted to painting, in order to express what writing alone cannot reach.

Preface to the Honzō Zufu (Illustrated Materia Medica)

It allows one to see everything clearly at a glance, leaving nothing hidden — this is precisely why such illustrations cannot be dispensed with. Therefore, those in the world who have spoken of materia medica, from Li Ji of the Tang and Su Song of the Song onward, have never failed to value such illustrated collections. By the time Li Shizhen of the Ming compiled his Bencao Gangmu (Compendium of Materia Medica), it magnificently gathered together the great achievements of all the various schools, and scholars since have taken it as their standard reference. However...

...its illustrations are in fact not worth looking at — why is this? I once obtained an original printing of the Gangmu and examined it. At the head of the volume it is recorded as "illustrations by Li Jianyuan," yet these illustrations were indeed not works of careful refinement. Moreover, through repeated copying and re-engraving over time, errors and crudeness crept in everywhere, so that in the end even Jianyuan's original work was lost. Is this not deeply regrettable! My friend Iwasaki Kanen, being deeply devoted [to this subject]...

Preface to the Illustrated Manual of Medicinal Plants, Volume One

The study of herbal medicine [lit. "the scholarship of the ochre whip," an allusion to Shennong]. He was also skilled at drawing from life, and had authored several volumes of a compendium on medicinal and animal subjects. Recently, concerning a certain category of plants, he engraved printing blocks and asked me to write a preface.

He had devoted himself earnestly to this field of study for nearly thirty years. He cultivated medicinal herbs in his garden plots, growing more than two thousand species, with hedges and fences, bamboo screens, and porcelain pots and jars all connected one after another. He wandered daily among his garden plantings,

personally tending and watering them, observing them closely and examining them in detail. He studied the forms and colors of their roots, stems, flowers, and fruits, and traced the changing states of their flourishing and withering. Whenever he gained insight into their nature, he would take up his brush and depict them, rendering them with great precision and fine detail, down to the minutest hair's breadth. He documented the similarities and differences in how they grew according to soil and region, including the distinct varieties found in deep, secluded cliffs and remote places, in order to

As for the fine and minute goods brought by trading ships from distant lands beyond the sea, they are all laid out before us, obtainable without even leaving one's desk—the diligence behind this may truly be called great. Now birds and beasts are things that mutually serve human use, yet the old classifications of livestock established in ancient times were not sufficient to elaborate fully on this subject; those who look into it cannot help but feel this as a regret.

This compilation by Kan'en, built upon the detailed structure of the Bencao Gangmu (Compendium of Materia Medica), has further gathered extensive research, making things as clear as if one were watching a fire, illuminating what was previously obscure and profound, so as to benefit students who come after. To call him a worthy successor and meritorious heir to Master Li (Li Shizhen)—who could possibly object to such a description?

Though I myself am not especially clever, I too have long taken an interest in this field of study. Having known Kan'en for a long time, I could not refuse his request, and so I have written this preface for him.

Preface to the Honzō Zufu

Among the things people love, none is loved more than life; among the things people hate, none is hated more than death. If one wishes to leave people without regret amid the crises of illness and the boundary between life and death, what other recourse is there but medicine? The Way of medicine is but one, yet its responsibility is extremely heavy and pressing. And in the course of administering treatment, nothing can be accomplished without reliance upon medicinal substances. The relationship between medicine and its materia medica is as urgent and indispensable as that between a general and his soldiers. Even if one has an excellent general or a miraculous physician, if he is left to stand with folded arms, he can only wait helplessly for the patient's decline and death.

[margin] Honzo Zufu, Volume 5, Miscellaneous Garden Plants

...only this. Therefore victory or defeat in battle depends on the quality of provisions, whether strong or weak, suitable or not; and whether medicines are of fine or coarse quality is likewise something one cannot but be careful about.

This is precisely why the study of medicinal herbs (honzōgaku) cannot be treated as anything but urgent and important. Since the sages of high antiquity first compiled its classics, every age has had those who recorded and transmitted it, until in the Ming dynasty Li Shizhen compiled and arranged it, bringing it to great completion. Yet although he searched thoroughly and composed his explanations, in gathering and preserving material his accounts were sometimes careless or mistaken, not a few; and at times he focused solely on flavor and energy (qi) while leaving gaps and omissions.

As for form and appearance — if one now tests this against the climates of East and West, large and small, thick and thin, good and bad already differ one from another; and if one does not truly know what a given thing is, shallow people will guess at it rashly and use it accordingly — there are such cases. Those who suffer harm from careless, unexamined application of it also exist. As for scholarship on this matter, failing to get its principles right is no small or trivial matter.

Then there appeared masters such as Wakamizu (若水稲先生), after whom this field of study became considerably clarified; and Kaibara, Matsuoka, Abe, Tamura, Ota, Ono and other teachers carried it further and made it flourish one after another. As a result, its theories became ever more refined and precise — though the pace of this advancement has been at times urgent, at times slow.

Honzo Zufu (Illustrated Herbal Compendium)
Volume 50

[The text] handed down [uses] written characters, yet how can one truly capture the image of a thing through words alone? To truly know an object, it must be like the time when Yu cast his bronze cauldrons so that people could recognize and avoid demons and monsters—only after seeing the actual form could they know it.

This is why mere words are insufficient to convey the essence—they cannot fully express the nature, temperament, and flavor of a thing the way that an image depicting its visible form can. Because the visible shape of a thing is best shown through pictures, this is the very reason why I have compiled this illustrated herbal.

Flowers and fruits, if not accurately rendered, may be mistaken for cats, and students who come after may fall into doubt and confusion as a result.

Illustrations may sometimes be imperfect and clumsy in execution, yet still convey some impression.

Honzo Zufu
Volume 50
Page 3

If one does not see something with one's own eyes, understanding remains unclear. Yet the world contains so many things, scattered across east and west, far and near, blooming and withering at different times, amid mountains and seas full of danger—how could one possibly see them all firsthand?

Thus images and words must work together—it cannot be otherwise. Of these three means [direct observation, verbal description, and illustration], each has its own particular day of use.

One cannot possibly provide illustrations for every single object in existence—there are always gaps. Verbal description also has its limits.

There is always one more layer removed in explanation; even if a description is extremely detailed, when one reads it, there remains a need to form a mental image from the words before true understanding is achieved, and even then doubts and confusions may linger.

But with illustrations, it is not so—one glance makes everything perfectly clear, with no need for further labor of the mind.

[The text reflects on inference and verification.]
One can see it, therefore in raising livestock one cannot be without precision and skill.
How can one distinguish what merely resembles [the genuine] from what is confused with it?
This is of great importance. In the world, physicians who act hastily in pursuit of gain fail to examine carefully.
That by which a physician is a physician is treated as dirt beneath dogs and horses, and so he regards other people's
life and death lightly. If someone reproaches him for it, he says it is fate,
and gives no further thought to the matter — how could he have leisure to weigh and select his medicines?
How much more true this is when it comes to the fine distinctions between the refined and the coarse in medicinal substances!
How indeed can one speak of it? And how much more so regarding the careful discernment between fineness and coarseness in the treatment of livestock!

Fascicle Four: Stored at the Razoku Garden

[The passage continues in a reflective tone about neglect and carelessness:]
Being at ease and abandoning urgent duties, one who has no leisure to make proper selections
lets the fine points perish — like a merchant's wife at the drug shop who never again asks whether what is genuine or false,
fine or coarse, has ever once been properly distinguished, so that things become mixed and confused.
Clearly, this proclaims the bias — being able to distinguish the subtlety of things, yet neglecting disputes and letting them go unresolved.
Is it fate or is it method or technique? Even in matters of lawsuits and litigation, the officials in charge
often fail to listen to things themselves, and instead let a single clique of corrupt clerks handle and decide
the cases — right is deemed wrong, and what is genuine is called false,
so that the common people quite simply have no one to show them leniency or fairness. This is truly a matter for deep sighing and lament.

Ever since my youth I have been fond of learning, always taking up the books of many scholars and reading them closely. Examining these matters, I probed deeply and, weighing the various theories, assigned each plant to its proper type—its seedlings, leaves, flowers, and fruit—sketching them from life according to the season, so that none of their peculiarities were missed.

I searched the mountains and wilds, transplanting specimens into garden plots and pots, in all more than two thousand kinds. Even from remote and out-of-the-way places, wherever my eyes beheld a plant I drew it without exception. In this way, over more than twenty years, I gradually completed a number of volumes, which I have titled "Honzō Bigafu" (Illustrated Compendium of Medicinal Plants). In making these illustrations I exhausted my skill to the utmost, applying color with the greatest care and devoting all my spirit to the work.

[As for the purpose of this work] — by consulting it even a child could, within a single glance, without wasting words or expense, distinguish what a certain object truly is. It would spare physicians of the world the trouble of hastily guessing at remedies, for by using it in their practice they could rely on it with confidence, judging that the name and substance of a plant are better established by careful comparison than left to guesswork. If it can be rightly applied to the treatment of illness, then perhaps the people of the whole realm — in matters of life, death, and fate — might be spared regret. In the critical moments between life and death, may this work preserve [something of value] for the world to come.

[Marginal title: Honzō Zufu, Volume 5]
[Collector's seal: Preserved in the Yakuen Collection]

[Title] Illustrated Treatise on Materia Medica (Honzō Zufu)

It may be called the "Untei" [pavilion of the hare/moon]—this is not mere idle self-indulgence, but the fruit of the esteemed scholar's devoted study and the deep learning he has long pursued.
I dare not claim to know with certainty the full fruits of his research and translations.
Though I am no scholar myself, I have had the chance to inquire into the refined labor of generations before setting this in order.
Those who wield the engraving knife have cut and trimmed the blocks to bring this work into proper sequence.
Written on a day in the tenth month, winter, of the year Bunsei 11 (1828), by Kan’en, Iwasaki Tsunemasa.

Illustrated Treatise on Materia Medica, Volume Five — Explanatory Notes

Explanatory Notes:

One: This book follows the sectional arrangement of the Bencao Gangmu (Compendium of Materia Medica), and begins with the mountain herbs, because among medicinal substances grasses and trees are the most numerous, and also because this section was compiled first. As for the illustrations of beasts, insects, fish and the like, they are not yet complete and will be supplied at a later date.

One: Although Chinese illustrated works on medicinal substances exist—such as the Beiji Bencao, the Erya Tu, and some thirty other illustrated compilations, as well as works like the Secretly Transmitted Flower Mirror—their accounts are sketchy and unclear, and they fail to capture the true appearance of things. As for the plants of our own country—mountain plants, field plants, flower collections, and so forth seen in various painted albums—most of them are rendered without color.

Even where coloring has been applied, the true appearance has not been captured, and none of them can be relied upon as accurate evidence. This illustrated treatise bases its forms on [illegible]...

After printing, I further commissioned a painter to apply colors. Although this careful checking does not lose accuracy, having an artisan apply color is costly; therefore the colored editions are made available only to those who wish to purchase and request them.

One: this book is centered on illustrations accompanied by explanatory notes. Above, the Chinese (kanji) name is given; below, the old Japanese names, common names, and current popular names are recorded. It also records, for each country and region, the shape, color, scent, taste, root, stem, flower, fruit, and growing season, so that people may easily recognize the plants.

One: for items whose actual specimens could be directly observed, all were sketched from life. As for foreign items such as spikenard, turmeric, nutmeg, and cloves, these were copied from specimens kept in the collection of Udagawa Yōan.

Western items are supplemented with Indian illustrations. Although both traditions have many types in common, since the Dutch sources contain more, these were added, each noted with its original book title and foreign name. Also, for illustrations of domestic (Japanese) products produced by other people, the source is noted alongside.

One: this book includes kana annotations beside the characters, so that mountain woodcutters and fishermen may easily understand them at a glance... discern as well. However, I fear that my wording is clumsy and crude—some things meant to be made clear remain obscure, and some meant to be corrected remain mistaken. I hope that learned gentlemen will kindly correct these errors.

One variety: Ryukyu Wa-umui

Commonly called "mokukyōka" (wood-apricot flower), in the Ryukyus it is also known by this name. Its branches resemble those of jasmine (sobi), and it blooms in summer with trailing flowers. Its shape resembles the "kayūka" flower, with yellow petals. Its fragrance and abundance are noted; in the "Kyōtsūshi" it is called "tanshunka" (spring-seeking flower). According to the commentary in the "Seiji-tsū," under the entry for "jakuji," it is said that in present-day Xiamen the jasmine flower is also called "gunshitsujaku" or "jutsushiki," and also known as "yashitsumitsu." Tulip (continued)

Udagawa Yōan [notes that] the "tulip" is cultivated in gardens of Holland and France;
the "tulip" is known by six different national names.
In Dutch it is called "tulp."
Its stem is round, with a soft pith inside, and grows to about a foot in height. The root sends up two or three leaves.
The leaves are broad, smooth, moist, and patterned with faint markings like brocade. At the tip of the stem
there are six large petals; the flower's shape is uniform, with three [per stem].
After flowering, the stem bears fruit; inside there are three chambers. Within the chambers
along the ridges, the seeds are red, purple, yellow, white, or other mixed colors.
The seeds are red, round, and flattened; the root is bulb-shaped and is yellow or sometimes black in color.

It flowers from the second to third month, in a form resembling crimson-blue (ai-beni).
From the fourth to fifth month, it bears fringed flowers, that is,
almond-like (an apricot scent/form).
